abstract: Welfare caseloads in North America halved following reforms in the 1990s and 2000s. We study how this shift affected families by linking Canadian welfare records to tax returns, medical care, educational attainment, and criminal charges. We find substantial and heterogeneous employment responses that increased average income despite reduced transfers. We find zero effects on aggregate healthcare costs, but mothers saw reduced preventative care and increased mental health treatment, consistent with the transition to employment elevating time pressure and stress. We find no effect on teenagers’ education or criminal charges as young adults but find some evidence of intergenerational welfare transmission.
title: The Effect of Reducing Welfare Access on Employment, Health, and Children’s Long-Run Outcomes

abstract: Women are significantly underrepresented in the technology sector. We design an experimental study using field data to identify the role of statistical discrimination in job applicant assessments. First, we measure the programming skills of job applicants for a programming job. Then, we recruit a large sample of employers consisting of human resource and tech professionals and incentivize them to predict the performance of these applicants based on their standardized resumes. We find no significant gender differences in programming skills. However, consistent with statistical discrimination we find employers perceive female applicants to be significantly less skilled. We also provide experimental evidence that the perceived gender skill gap can be readily eliminated. Employers who were randomized to have access to additional information such as aptitude or personality do not believe that there are gender differences in programming skills. Together, these findings suggest that tech employers believe women are less skilled programmers. Nonetheless, in the context of hiring, the scope for statistical discrimination may be limited in practice as employers often have access to more information when assessing applicants.
journal: Journal of the European Economic Association
title: The Scope of Statistical Discrimination: An Experimental Study on Gender Barriers in Tech,

abstract: This paper investigates the causal impact of local land-use regulations on the deployment of wind and solar energy systems and their subsequent effects on county-level economic activity in Indiana. Since 2008, Indiana's renewable energy capacity has grown to 12% of total generation, yet this expansion is governed by a highly decentralized regulatory framework. Using a two-way fixed effects difference-in-difference (DiD) panel analysis from 2001 to 2021, we examine how restrictive local regulations influence GDP and employment across multiple sectors. Our findings reveal significant sectoral reallocations. While wind and solar restrictions slightly bolster agricultural GDP, they exert a pronounced negative effect on utilities, durable goods manufacturing, and the information sector. Specifically, the results suggest that de facto restrictions on Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) stifle industrial expansion, as modern firms increasingly require proximity to renewable sources to meet sustainability targets. Spatial econometric tests further demonstrate that these regulations drive utility investment into adjacent counties while simultaneously reducing regional manufacturing and information-sector growth. These results highlight a critical trade-off for policymakers between local land-use autonomy and the ability to attract high-value, energy-dependent capital investment in an increasingly decarbonized economy.
title: Towards the economic effects of renewable energy restrictions: Evidence from Indiana, USA

abstract: The rapid expansion of utility-scale ground-mounted photovoltaics (PV) in Poland has intensified competition for agricultural land at a time when the spatial planning system that governs where such installations may be sited is itself being reformed. This article develops and applies four diagnostic indicators of land-use pressure: the regional concentration of installed PV capacity, a land-take intensity coefficient, a land-rent capitalisation rate, and the gap between the initiation and the formal adoption of the municipal general plans required under Poland's 2023 planning reform. The indicators are computed from national statistical, energy-regulatory and land-agency data for Poland and Lithuania. Installed capacity is dispersed at the national scale but markedly asymmetric between regions: Wielkopolskie holds 23.1% of national capacity on 9.5% of national territory, and the five leading voivodeships together account for 55.9%. Lease rents offered for PV siting correspond to 11.5–57.6% of land value and are seven to thirteen times the national average rent obtained for agricultural leases of state land. Only 1.3% of Polish municipalities had formally adopted a general plan by March 2026; although the share rose to 35.37% by the 31 August 2026 deadline, most municipalities still lacked an adopted general plan. The benchmark applied is Poland's own statutory planning timetable, not a generic concentration standard. The indicators capture land-use pressure and institutional bottlenecks rather than observed conflict, and the relationships reported are associative. Lithuania's legal recognition of dual agricultural and energy land use is treated as an institutional benchmark rather than a directly transferable model.
title: Solar farms and agricultural land competition in Poland and Lithuania: Spatial concentration, land rent and planning implementation gaps

abstract: Homelessness is associated with an immense health burden and limited access to adequate healthcare. This paper studies the effects of Mobile Street Clinics on healthcare usage among people experiencing homelessness in Brazil. Exploiting unique administrative data in a staggered difference-in-differences setting, I find that Mobile Street Clinics strongly and persistently increase primary care usage and psycho-social care usage among people experiencing homelessness but do not improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes. These results suggest that MSCs expand healthcare access and utilization, but that expanding access alone is not sufficient to improve treatment continuity.
title: Increasing healthcare usage among the homeless: Evidence from Mobile Street Clinics in Brazil

abstract: Recent theoretical models challenge probability weighting function as it was originally conceived in Prospect Theory in ways that are not straightforward to test using choice data. This study addresses these constraints by measuring neural responses to probability. Utilizing a unique dataset comprising 64,175 decision trials and 78,067 neural measurement trials, we pinpoint neurons whose activity (a basic biological decision processing unit) responds to probability, but does not detectably respond to payoff magnitudes, supporting the economic assumption that probabilities and utilities are in principle separable. Our observed neural probability-response functions are S-shaped, which we show can maximize earnings in our experimental environment, but diverge from probability weighting estimated from behavior under conventional assumptions. Incorporating biologically realistic, context-dependent utility in the estimation produces estimates that are more closely aligned with the independently measured neural probability-response function.
title: Neural and behavioral probability weighting function

abstract: Entrepreneurship is a key livelihood strategy for internal migrants in developing countries, yet its viability is increasingly threatened by intensifying climate shocks. This study examines the impact of tropical storms on entrepreneurial activity among internal migrants. We find that storm exposure significantly reduces entrepreneurship, suggesting an annual decline of approximately 98,385 entrepreneurial activities and potentially associated economic losses of about USD 136 million, with effects that appear to persist for at least two years. The observed patterns are consistent with the role of post-storm asset losses faced by migrants. We further document suggestive evidence of heterogeneity across gender, age, education, and employment sectors. Finally, we find that greater urban drainage density and higher road area per capita are associated with weaker impacts, indicating a possible mitigating role of urban infrastructure.

abstract: I study costly inspections of a firm whose effort affects persistent quality and whose revenue depends on reputation. Full effort is globally optimal if and only if inspection costs do not exceed a computable cutoff. Above it, I construct a sequence of policies that strictly improve on the best full-effort policy. Their payoff gains and expected discounted effort losses vanish, but the gain-to-loss ratio diverges. No finite additional linear weight on quality restores full-effort optimality. The result allows nonlinear effort costs and asymmetric information losses.
title: Optimality of full effort in dynamic monitoring

abstract: Extreme heatwaves can undermine the efficiency of fossil-fuel power generation, amplifying air pollution and health risks. Using plant-level operational data and high-resolution weather data from China, we find that during the 2022 extreme heatwave in Guangdong Province, exposed plants experienced approximately 21.4% higher PM2.5 emission intensity relative to unexposed plants, an increase attributable to heatwave-induced efficiency losses. Coal-fired plants exhibited an additional 12.3% increase relative to gas-fired plants. Similar patterns are observed for other combustion-related pollutants. We estimate that heatwave-induced pollution from power-sector efficiency losses imposes an annual social cost of USD 4.21 billion in China, which could be reduced by USD 1.42 billion under a complete coal-to-gas substitution scenario. Looking ahead, under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, which is associated with approximately 4.4 °C of warming by 2100, annual costs in China could rise to USD 20.41 billion. The impacts are highly uneven across provinces, with coal-dependent and industrial coastal regions disproportionately affected. Our findings highlight how extreme heatwaves can amplify air pollution and health damages through an overlooked energy-sector efficiency channel, underscoring the broader societal costs of continued fossil-fuel dependence in a warming world.

abstract: We develop a model averaging approach for impulse response estimation in vector autoregressions (VARs) to circumvent lag-order uncertainty. Unlike existing VAR model averaging approaches that primarily focus on prediction accuracy, the proposed weight determination criterion is based on coefficient estimation accuracy. We show that when a correct model is included among the candidates, the resulting weights on the correct models converge to one and the averaging estimators are consistent. Regardless of whether a correct model is included among the candidates, the estimated weights converge to the optimal weights that minimize the expected quadratic error of the estimator. A sieve bootstrap procedure is further developed for inference. Simulation results demonstrate competitive performance and provide practical guidance for implementing the method. An empirical application investigating the output–inflation trade-off suggests that contractionary monetary policy can mitigate inflationary pressures while its adverse impact on output may be less severe.
title: Model averaging estimator of impulse responses in vector autoregressions

abstract: How does structural change in global value chains reshape systemic vulnerability? Using the OECD Inter-Country Input–Output Extended database (1995–2022), this study reconceptualizes systemic vulnerability through two distinct dimensions: ‘fragility’ and ‘amplification’. The results reveal a structural decoupling in which ‘fragility’ declines over time while ‘amplification’ increases and becomes more volatile. This pattern suggests that increasing integration can simultaneously enhance aggregate stability and strengthen propagation capacity. Further analysis indicates that increasing interdependence improves buffering capacity, whereas declining modularity and expanding core structures intensify cascading propagation. These findings challenge the view that deeper integration uniformly enhances resilience and demonstrate that structural transformation simultaneously strengthens risk-sharing and propagation mechanisms. The study highlights the need to move beyond outcome-based measures and adopt structurally grounded approaches to assessing systemic vulnerability in highly interconnected economies.
title: Structural decoupling in global value chains: Divergent dynamics of fragility and amplification

abstract: Liquidity premia on near-money assets (e.g. Treasury bills) co-move positively with monetary policy rates, a pattern usually read as the opportunity cost of money. I show that a cost-minimizing Treasury tilts issuance toward bills when policy eases, so part of the co-movement is issuance-mediated. A minimal model maps instrumental-variable regressions into a decomposition of the pass-through. Estimating the issuance response directly, point estimates attribute roughly one quarter of the effect of the policy rate on the premium to endogenous bill supply. The results inform the determination of US assets’ liquidity premia, an increasingly central input in macro and finance.
title: Monetary policy, endogenous bill supply, and the liquidity premium

abstract: This paper examines how export demand shocks affect firms' export portfolios and, through within‐firm product reallocation, promote the productivity of multi‐product firms. Combining Chinese micro‐level data with global bilateral trade data from 2000 to 2007, this paper constructs measures of destination‐specific export demand shocks and export skewness. We find that positive export demand shocks in foreign markets induce firms to concentrate a larger share of their export sales in better‐performing products. This finding is robust to alternative measures of export skewness, potential sample selection concerns and controls for changes in trade policy. Furthermore, positive export demand shocks are associated with higher firm productivity, and the evidence suggests that increased export concentration constitutes an important channel underlying these productivity gains. Consistent with a within‐firm reallocation mechanism, the productivity‐enhancing effect of export demand shocks is concentrated exclusively among multi‐product firms.

abstract: We estimate the effect of official language adoption on bilateral exports using a difference‐in‐differences design that exploits 49 policy changes across 31 countries (1996–2019). With exporter‐year, importer‐year and country‐pair fixed effects, PPML estimates imply that sharing a newly adopted official language increases exports by 20.6%. Event studies show no pre‐trends, and placebo tests suggest the effect is unlikely to reflect spurious correlation. The effect is concentrated in communication‐intensive sectors (those with high O*NET communication scores, high contract intensity and differentiated products), consistent with reduced information frictions rather than political alignment. A general‐equilibrium counterfactual maps the estimate to a 2.91% reduction in ad valorem trade costs.
title: Linguistic Bridge: The Impact of New Official Languages on International Trade

abstract: The investment boom in artificial intelligence technologies has raised concerns about a potential bubble. This column argues that the 1920s boom and the Great Depression offer useful lessons. During the 1920s, process innovation grew rapidly, while product innovation stagnated. In turn, process innovation fuelled an investment boom based on an expectation of future demand. When this expectation failed to materialise, a sharp contraction followed. Thus, the optimism and prosperity of the Roaring Twenties help explain the onset of the Great Depression, and offer a cautionary tale for today’s artificial intelligence boom.
authors: Harold Cole, Stefano Cravero, Jeremy Greenwood
title: The boom before the bust: From the Roaring Twenties to the Great Depression

abstract: Stablecoins could make payments and remittances cheaper and faster, but policymakers worry they could also help residents, particularly in emerging markets, circumvent capital controls and move savings into US dollars. This column introduces estimates of stablecoin flows and holdings for 188 countries, built from public blockchain data. Emerging market and developing economies take part in 86% of cross-border stablecoin flows and hold about three quarters of stablecoins. Cross-border stablecoin activity rises by roughly 30% after countries tighten restrictions on capital outflows and shows no sign of falling back when they are lifted. Holdings rise by roughly 75% in the year after a currency crisis begins and then persist.

abstract: Rural revitalization has become a long-term national strategy in China, placing new demands on rural land use research and territorial spatial planning. Within this context, accurately identifying the location and scope of administrative villages serves as a fundamental data prerequisite. However, the acquisition of spatial data for administrative villages is usually complicated, time-consuming, low- accuracy, and subject to significant human subjectivity. To address this gap, this study developed an intelligent extraction framework for administrative villages. Taking three counties in the Yan River basin on the Loess Plateau of China as a case study, this study extracted rural settlement patches using a Random Forest Classifier (RFC), classified these patches as administrative villages using a Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) to identify their locations, and delineated their spatial scope using Voronoi diagrams. The results showed: 1) The framework identified more than 19,000 rural settlement patches and 1864 administrative villages, with an administrative village identification accuracy exceeding 95% based on validation samples. 2) The spatial distribution of administrative villages exhibited distinct spatial patterns associated with terrain, roads, and rivers. 3) The scope of administrative villages exhibited spatial heterogeneity across different loess geomorphic settings. The resulting administrative village spatial data could provide a spatial basis for rural reconstruction and the identification of differentiated village development types, supporting targeted land use planning and rural revitalization strategies.

abstract: We introduce a unifying stability concept to cooperative game theorythe equity equilibrium. A central authority selects an outcome of the game to enforce and evaluates its stability using a collection of functions called a complaint system.These complaints are used to identify the grievances against and the concessions to each player. Equity equilibrium occurs when an individually rational payo¤ con guration balances the grievances and concessions of each player. We establish the existence of equity equilibrium for any valid complaint system and under any coalition structure. Next, we show that equity equilibrium under speci c complaint systems characterizes the kernel, the Shapley value, and the generalized Nash bargaining solution of a cooperative game. We show how simplicial algorithms can be employed for computing any type of equity equilibrium. This approach is illustrated with an example from the Tennessee Valley Authority.
title: Equity Equilibrium for Cooperative Games

abstract: Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) account for an increasingly large share of credit provision and play a central role in quantitative easing (QE). We develop a DSGE model with banks, NBFIs and a central bank interacting through wholesale deposits, bonds and reserve markets to study how monetary transmission changes as the size of NBFIs expands. We estimate the model on UK data to evaluate key parameters in the financial sector. We find that the transmission of conventional interest rate policy to output and inflation is essentially unaffected by the size of the NBFI sector. Conversely, the transmission of QE is strongly altered by the size of the NBFI sector and the source of its expansion. When the NBFI sector expands due to firm funding preferences, this amplifies QE. When it expands due to an increased cost of obtaining bank finance, transmission is largely unchanged. The results underscore that monetary policymakers retain rate control regardless of financial structure, but that the effectiveness of balance sheet policies depends on the composition and behaviour of the non-bank sector.
authors: Nicolò Bandera & Kristina Bluwstein & Michael Kumhof & Mauricio Salgado-Moreno & Jacob Stevens
title: Lighting the shadows: central bank policy transmission through banks and non-banks
